decks.title: Topographical Maps: Colours, Symbols, Scale, Distance and Direction, Part 1: Colours, symbols and scale
goals: State what each colour tint on a topographical sheet shows
Recognise the common conventional symbols for settlements, water, roads and tracks
Name the three types of scale and convert a statement scale to a representative fraction and back

slides.heading: The language of a topographical sheet
slides.body_md: A topographical sheet carries a lot of information in a small space, so the survey uses **colours** and **symbols** that mean the same thing on every sheet. A **scale** tells you how the map shrinks the ground. This chapter uses the **imagined practice sheet** (not a real place, not a Survey of India sheet) to learn all three.

rows: The kind of land or feature
A single object, such as a well or a road
How far the ground distance is for each map distance

visual.alt: Table of three ideas of the chapter: colour, symbol and scale
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: A topographical sheet packs a lot of information into a small space. It does this with colours, with symbols and with a scale. The colours and symbols mean the same thing on every sheet. The scale tells you how the ground has been shrunk to fit on paper. In this chapter we use our imagined practice sheet to learn all three.

slides.heading: Colour tints and what they show
slides.body_md: By the usual convention: **yellow** is **cultivated land**, **green** is **forest** (and orchards), **white** is **uncultivated** land such as open scrub or barren ground, **blue** is **water** (streams, tanks, canals), **brown** is **relief** (contours), **black** is man-made features such as huts, tracks and names, and **red** is used for **metalled roads**. On the imagined sheet by area: cultivated 45%, open scrub 33%, forest 22%.

rows: The conical hill and the ridge

visual.alt: Table of seven colours on the sheet, what each shows and an example from the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Each colour has a job. Yellow shows cultivated land. Green shows forest. White shows land that is not farmed, such as open scrub. Blue is for water, brown is for contours, black is for huts, tracks and names, and red is for metalled roads. On our imagined sheet nearly half the area is yellow, a third is white and about a fifth is green.

slides.heading: Reading the key of the sheet
slides.body_md: Every sheet has a **key** (legend) that lists its symbols. Always check the key before you answer. The key of the imagined practice sheet is printed below the map. It shows the line symbols, the point symbols and the colour tints used on this sheet.

visual.alt: Full imagined practice sheet with its key. Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet.
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Every sheet comes with a key. It lists every symbol and tint used on that sheet. Before you answer any question, find the symbol in the key and read what it means. Here the key is printed below our imagined sheet. It shows the lines, the points and the colours that we use in this chapter.

slides.heading: Point symbols: settlements, services and water
slides.body_md: **Huts** are small black squares: close together they form a **settlement**, scattered they are **dispersed huts**. A **temple** is a small flag on a square, a **well** is a circle with a dot, and a **tank** is a blue shape. **PO** marks a post office, **PS** a police station and **Dis** a dispensary. Black **triangles** and **dots** with figures are triangulated and spot heights.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet with labelled symbols: temple, huts of Nandiwadi, police station, post office, well, a river, a canal and a footpath
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Now the point symbols. Small black squares are huts. Close together they make a village, and scattered they are dispersed huts. A temple is a flag on a small square, and a well is a circle with a dot. The letters PO, PS and Dis stand for post office, police station and dispensary. A tank, which is a small lake, is drawn in blue.

slides.heading: Quick check: colours
slides.body_md: Match a colour tint to what it shows.
slides.narration: Quick check. Yellow tint is cultivated land and green tint is forest.

slides.heading: Line symbols: roads, tracks, streams and canals
slides.body_md: **Roads:** a **metalled road** is a thick **red** line; an **unmetalled road** is a thick black broken line; a **cart track** is a thin black line; a **pack track** is a thin broken line; a **footpath** is a dotted line. **Water lines:** a **perennial stream** is a continuous blue line, a **seasonal stream** is a **dashed** blue line, a **canal** is a thick blue line that follows a contour. A short thick bar across a river on a road is a **bridge**.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet showing a metalled road with a bridge, an unmetalled road, cart track, footpaths, a river, a canal and a seasonal stream
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Line symbols come next. A metalled road is thick and red. An unmetalled road is thick, black and broken. A cart track is a thin black line, a pack track is thin and broken, and a footpath is a line of dots. In blue, a stream that flows all year is a solid line, a seasonal stream is dashed, and a canal is a thick line that follows a contour. A short bar across a river is a bridge.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming features from symbols
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In the extract, name (a) the thick red line, (b) the dashed blue line, (c) the dotted black line, (d) the black square with a flag.

**(a)** Metalled road (red, thick).

**(b)** Seasonal stream (blue, dashed): it carries water only in the rains.

**(c)** Footpath (black dots).

**(d)** Temple (flag on a square).

visual.alt: Table of four symbols from the extract with the feature each shows
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Let us name some features. A thick red line is a metalled road. A dashed blue line is a seasonal stream, which carries water only in the rains. A dotted black line is a footpath. A small flag on a black square is a temple. For each one, quote the symbol and then say what it means.

slides.heading: Three kinds of scale
slides.body_md: The **scale** of a map is the relation between a distance on the map and the same distance on the ground. There are three ways to state it. **Statement scale:** in words, such as **1 cm to 0.5 km**. **Representative fraction (RF):** a ratio with no units, **1 : 50 000**. **Linear scale:** a **bar** divided into km (and tenths) that you can measure against. The imagined sheet uses all three, and one grid square (1 km) is **2 cm** on a printed sheet.

visual.alt: Table of the three types of scale and how each appears on the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: A scale tells you how the ground has been shrunk. There are three ways to give it. A statement scale uses words, like one centimetre to half a kilometre. A representative fraction is a ratio with no units, like one to fifty thousand. A linear scale is a bar marked in kilometres that you can measure against. Our imagined sheet shows all three.

slides.heading: Worked example: statement scale to representative fraction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert the statement scale **1 cm to 0.5 km** to a representative fraction.

**Step 1.** Convert the ground distance to centimetres: 0.5 km = 0.5 × 1 000 × 100 = **50 000 cm**.

**Step 2.** So 1 cm on the map stands for 50 000 cm on the ground.

**Step 3.** RF = 1 : 50 000.

Check with another scale: 2 cm to 1 km: 1 km = 100 000 cm, so 1 cm stands for 50 000 cm: RF 1 : 50 000 again.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for converting a statement scale into a representative fraction
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: To change a statement scale into a representative fraction, put both distances in centimetres. Half a kilometre is five hundred metres, which is fifty thousand centimetres. So one centimetre on the map stands for fifty thousand centimetres on the ground. The representative fraction is one to fifty thousand. Two centimetres to one kilometre gives the same ratio.

slides.heading: Quick check: representative fraction
slides.body_md: Convert a statement scale to an RF.
slides.narration: Quick check. Change the ground distance to centimetres and write one to that number.

slides.heading: The linear scale
slides.body_md: A **linear scale** is a bar divided into equal parts, each standing for a ground distance. The first division is usually split into tenths so that small distances can be read. On the extract the bar is **5 km** long and each black or white block is **1 km**, the same length as one grid square. To use it, mark the map distance on a strip of paper and lay the strip on the bar.

slides.narration: This is a linear scale. It is a bar divided into equal blocks, and each block stands for one kilometre here. The same length is one grid square. To use it, mark the distance on a strip of paper and lay the strip along the bar, then read off the kilometres. A linear scale is useful because it stays correct even if the map is enlarged or reduced.

slides.heading: Worked example: representative fraction to statement scale
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sheet has an RF of **1 : 25 000**. Write its statement scale.

**Step 1.** 1 cm on the map stands for 25 000 cm on the ground.

**Step 2.** 25 000 cm = 250 m = **0.25 km**.

**Step 3.** Statement scale: **1 cm to 0.25 km**. (At 1 : 100 000, 1 cm would stand for 1 km.)

visual.alt: Table of three representative fractions with their statement scales
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Now the other way. A map has a representative fraction of one to twenty five thousand. One centimetre on the map stands for twenty five thousand centimetres on the ground. That is two hundred and fifty metres, or a quarter of a kilometre. So the statement scale is one centimetre to point two five kilometres. A smaller second number means a larger scale map.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Colours show the kind of land or feature, and the key explains each symbol. The three kinds of scale are the statement scale, the representative fraction and the linear scale. To change a statement scale into a representative fraction, put the ground distance in centimetres. On our sheet every centimetre on the map is half a kilometre on the ground.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Quote both the colour and the feature: "yellow: cultivated land".
Write an RF with no units: 1 : 50 000, not 1 cm : 50 000 cm.
Show the unit conversion (km to cm) when you work out an RF.
Always check the key; two sheets may use slightly different symbols.

slides.narration: Some tips. Say both the colour and the feature, for example yellow means cultivated land. Write a representative fraction without units. When you convert a scale, show the change from kilometres to centimetres, because one kilometre is one lakh centimetres. And always look at the key before you answer, because it is the final word on a symbol.

decks.title: Topographical Maps: Colours, Symbols, Scale, Distance and Direction, Part 2: Distance, area and direction
goals: Calculate the straight-line distance between two places using the scale
Calculate the area of a region from full grid squares only
State the direction of one place from another using the eight points of the compass

slides.heading: Measuring on the sheet
slides.body_md: With the scale you can turn map measurements into ground measurements. In the ICSE paper you only measure **straight-line (direct) distance**, you find **area** only from **complete grid squares**, and you give **direction** with the **eight points of the compass**. We practise all three on the imagined practice sheet.

rows: Straight line, then use the scale
N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW

visual.alt: Table of the three measurements of the chapter and how each is made
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Now we measure on the sheet. We use the scale to turn map distances into ground distances, but only in a straight line. We find area by counting complete grid squares only. And we give directions using the eight points of the compass. All the examples use our imagined practice sheet.

slides.heading: Straight-line distance
slides.body_md: To find the **direct (straight-line) distance** between two places: join them with a straight line; measure it in **cm** with a ruler (or on a strip of paper against the **linear scale**); multiply by the scale (here **0.5 km per cm**). On the extract the police station A and the temple B are about **1.8 cm** apart on a printed sheet, so the ground distance is about **0.9 km**. Roads and rivers are not measured here, only straight lines.

slides.narration: To find the straight line distance between two places, join them with a straight line and measure it with a ruler. Then multiply the centimetres by the scale. On this sheet every centimetre stands for half a kilometre. The police station and the temple are about one point eight centimetres apart on a printed sheet, so the ground distance is about nine tenths of a kilometre.

slides.heading: Worked example: Sonakhedi to the temple
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** On a printed sheet the centre of Sonakhedi (S) and the temple (T) are about 7.9 cm apart. Find the ground distance.

**Step 1.** Scale: 1 cm to 0.5 km.

**Step 2.** Distance = 7.9 × 0.5 = **3.95 km**, about **4 km**.

**Check with the grid.** S and T differ by 3.25 km east-west and 2.25 km north-south, so the distance is √(3.25² + 2.25²) = 3.95 km.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet with Sonakhedi marked S and the temple marked T and a linear scale bar
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Let us work an example. Sonakhedi and the temple are about seven point nine centimetres apart on a printed sheet. Multiply by the scale of half a kilometre per centimetre and you get three point nine five kilometres, which is about four kilometres. You can check this from the grid, because the two places are three and a quarter kilometres apart east to west and two and a quarter kilometres north to south.

slides.heading: Area from full grid squares
slides.body_md: Every grid square is 1 km by 1 km, so it covers **1 sq km**. To find the area of a region, count only the **complete squares** that the region covers and give the number as **sq km**. Squares that are only partly covered are **not** counted in this course. On the extract, the **yellow** cultivated land fills a block of 3 squares by 3 squares (eastings 45 to 48, northings 73 to 76): **9 full squares**, so the area is **9 sq km**.

visual.alt: Extract of the imagined practice sheet, squares 4573 to 4775, all covered by yellow cultivated land
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Each grid square covers one square kilometre. To find an area, count only the complete squares the region fills, and write the number in square kilometres. Part squares are not counted in this course. In the extract the yellow cultivated land fills a block three squares wide and three squares high, so it has nine complete squares and an area of nine square kilometres.

slides.heading: Worked example: area of forest
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the area of forest (green) in the block between eastings 43 and 47 and northings 78 and 80 that fills **complete** squares.

**Step 1.** Look at each square in the block: the squares 4378, 4478, 4578, 4579, 4678, 4679 are wholly green.

**Step 2.** Count them: **6** full squares.

**Step 3.** Area = 6 × 1 sq km = **6 sq km**. Squares only partly green are left out.

visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: Now the forest. In the block between easting forty three and forty seven, and northing seventy eight and eighty, we look at each square. Six of them are wholly green. We count those six and leave out the squares that are only partly green. Each full square is one square kilometre, so the forest area is six square kilometres.

slides.body_md: Find an area from complete grid squares.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count only complete squares, each one square kilometre.

slides.heading: The eight points of the compass
slides.body_md: The four **cardinal points** are north (N), east (E), south (S) and west (W). The four **intercardinal points** lie between them: north-east (NE), south-east (SE), south-west (SW) and north-west (NW). On a topographical sheet **north is at the top** unless an arrow says otherwise, so east is to the right, south down and west to the left. Each point covers 45° of the circle.

slides.narration: The compass has four main points: north, east, south and west. Between them are north east, south east, south west and north west. On a topographical sheet north is at the top, so east is to the right, south is at the bottom and west is to the left. Each of the eight points covers forty five degrees of the circle.

slides.heading: Giving the direction of one place from another
slides.body_md: Name the direction **from** the first place **to** the second. Draw a line from the first to the second and see which of the eight points it follows. From the police station the temple lies **north**. Reverse the two places and the direction reverses: the police station is **south** of the temple.

visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet, not a real place and not a Survey of India sheet

slides.narration: To give a direction, say which way you must go from the first place to reach the second. Draw a line between them and see which of the eight points it follows. From the police station the temple lies to the north. If you reverse the two places, the direction reverses, so the police station lies to the south of the temple.

slides.heading: Worked example: direction and distance together
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In which direction is the temple (T) from the dispensary (D), and how far?

**Step 1.** The temple is 3.2 km east and 2.0 km north of D, so the line points between north and east: **north-east**.

**Step 2.** Distance = √(3.2² + 2.0²) = **3.8 km**.

**Answer.** The temple is about 3.8 km **north-east** of the dispensary; the dispensary is south-west of the temple.

slides.narration: Let us find the direction from the dispensary to the temple. The temple is about three kilometres east and two kilometres north of the dispensary, so the line points between north and east. That is north east. The distance, found from the two sides, is about three point eight kilometres. So the temple is three point eight kilometres north east of the dispensary.

notes.title: Topographical Maps: Colours, Symbols, Scale, Distance and Direction: Notes

sections.heading: 1. Colour tints
sections.body_md:
- **Yellow:** cultivated land. **Green:** forest (and orchards). **White:** uncultivated land such as open scrub or barren ground.
- **Blue:** water (streams, tanks, canals). **Brown:** relief, shown by contours. **Black:** man-made features: huts, tracks, names. **Red:** metalled roads. Real Survey of India sheets differ in some details (for example the colour of grid lines and settlements); follow the key printed on the sheet you are given.
- On the imagined practice sheet (not a real place, not a Survey of India sheet) about 45% of the area is cultivated, 33% open scrub and 22% forest.
- Always read the key of the sheet.

sections.heading: 2. Conventional symbols: points
sections.body_md:
- **Huts:** small black squares (clustered in a village or dispersed).
- **Temple:** flag on a square. **Well:** circle with a dot. **Tank:** blue shape.
- **PO** post office, **PS** police station, **Dis** dispensary.
- **Triangulated height:** black triangle with a figure. **Spot height:** black dot with a figure.

key_terms.definition_md: A standard sign that shows an object on a map without drawing it to scale.

sections.heading: 3. Conventional symbols: lines
sections.body_md:
- **Metalled road:** thick red line. **Unmetalled road:** thick black broken line. **Cart track:** thin black line. **Pack track:** thin broken line. **Footpath:** dotted line.
- **Perennial stream:** continuous blue line. **Seasonal stream:** dashed blue line. **Canal:** thick blue line along a contour. **Embankment:** line with short ticks. **Bridge:** short thick bar across the river.

key_terms.definition_md: A road with a hard surface of stone or tar, shown in red.
A stream that carries water only in the rains, shown by a dashed blue line.

sections.heading: 4. Scale
sections.body_md:
- **Statement scale:** in words (1 cm to 0.5 km). **Representative fraction (RF):** a ratio with no units (1 : 50 000). **Linear scale:** a bar marked in km.
- Statement scale to RF: convert the ground distance to cm. 0.5 km = 50 000 cm, so RF 1 : 50 000.
- RF to statement: 1 : 25 000 means 1 cm to 25 000 cm = 0.25 km.
- 1 km = 1 000 m = 100 000 cm. On the imagined sheet one grid square (1 km) is 2 cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The scale written as a ratio without units, such as 1 : 50 000.
A bar divided into ground distances, usable at any enlargement.

visual.alt: Table of the three scales of the imagined sheet
visual.caption: Imagined practice sheet

sections.heading: 5. Distance and area
sections.body_md:
- **Distance:** only the straight-line (direct) distance is measured. Measure in cm and multiply by 0.5 km per cm. For example 1.8 cm is 0.9 km. A check from the grid: distance = square root of (east-west difference squared plus north-south difference squared).
- **Area:** count only complete 1 km squares; each is 1 sq km. A block 3 squares by 3 squares has 9 sq km. Part squares are not counted.

key_terms.definition_md: The straight-line distance between two places, not along a road or river.

rows: Number of full squares gives sq km

sections.heading: 6. Direction
sections.body_md:
- Eight points: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW (45 degrees apart). North is at the top of a sheet unless an arrow shows otherwise.
- Give the direction from the first place to the second. Reversing the places gives the opposite point (NE becomes SW).
- On the imagined sheet the temple is north-east of the dispensary and about 3.8 km away; the police station is south of the temple.

key_terms.definition_md: North-east, south-east, south-west and north-west, between the four cardinal points.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing units in an RF, or forgetting to convert km to cm.
- Measuring distance along a road instead of the straight line.
- Counting part squares when finding area.
- Giving a direction from the second place to the first.
- Confusing seasonal (dashed) and perennial (continuous) streams.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Colour or symbol (1 mark): the feature, not just the colour.
- Scale (1 to 2 marks): the unit conversion shown and the RF written correctly.
- Distance, area (2 marks): working and unit.
- Direction (1 mark): one of the eight points.

questions.stem_md:
Study the extract of the imagined practice sheet in which S is the centre of Sonakhedi and T is the temple. (a) State the scale of the sheet as a representative fraction. [2]

(b) S and T are 7.9 cm apart on a printed sheet. Calculate the ground distance. [2]

(c) Check your answer from the grid, given that T is 3.25 km east and 2.25 km north of S. [3]

(d) State the direction of T from S and name the type of distance you measured. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1 cm to 0.5 km: 0.5 km = 50 000 cm, so the RF is 1 : 50 000.

(b) 7.9 × 0.5 = 3.95 km, about 4 km.

(c) Distance = √(3.25² + 2.25²) = √15.63 = 3.95 km, which agrees with part (b).

(d) T lies to the north-east of S. The distance measured is the direct (straight-line) distance.

questions.solution_md: RF; 3.95 km; check 3.95 km; north-east and straight-line.

questions.stem_md:
Study the extracts of the imagined practice sheet that show the cultivated land (yellow) in the south and the open scrub (white) in the west. (a) State what the yellow and white tints show. [2]

(b) Calculate the area of the yellow block between eastings 43 and 48 and northings 70 and 73, from its complete squares. [2]

(c) Calculate the area of the white block between eastings 40 and 44 and northings 74 and 76, and say how much larger the yellow block is. [3]

(d) Explain why only complete squares are counted and give the unit of your answers. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Yellow shows cultivated land; white shows uncultivated land (open scrub).

(b) 5 squares by 3 squares: 15 sq km.

(c) 4 squares by 2 squares: 8 sq km. The yellow block is 15 − 8 = 7 sq km larger.

(d) Each complete square stands for exactly 1 sq km, so counting complete squares gives a clear whole number; part squares are not counted in this course. The unit is the square kilometre (sq km).

questions.solution_md: Cultivated and uncultivated; 15 sq km; 8 sq km and 7 sq km larger; rule and unit.

questions.stem_md:
Study the extract of the imagined practice sheet in which the lines K, L, M and N are marked, and the full sheet with its key. (a) Name the features shown by K and L. [2]

(b) Name M and N and describe the symbol of each. [2]

(c) State the meaning of the yellow, green and blue colours on the sheet. [3]

(d) Explain why you should always read the key before answering a map question. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) K is a metalled road and L is a canal.

(b) M is a footpath, a dotted black line; N is an unmetalled road, a thick black broken line.

(c) Yellow shows cultivated land, green shows forest and blue shows water (streams, canal, tank).

(d) The key lists every symbol and tint used on that sheet and its meaning, so reading it prevents wrong identification; symbols can differ between sheets, and the key is the final authority.

questions.solution_md: Road and canal; footpath and unmetalled road; three colours; key explains symbols.

questions.stem_md:
Study the extracts of the imagined practice sheet. In the first, D is the dispensary and T is the temple; in the second, A is the centre of Pathrali and B is the police station. (a) State the direction of T from D. [2]

(b) State the direction of D from T. [2]

(c) Calculate the straight-line distance from D to T, given 3.2 km east and 2.0 km north, to 1 decimal place. [3]

(d) State the direction of B from A and its reverse, and explain how the two are related. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) North-east.

(b) South-west.

(c) √(3.2² + 2.0²) = √14.24 = 3.8 km.

(d) B is to the south-east of A, and A is to the north-west of B. Reversing the two places reverses the direction to the opposite compass point.

questions.solution_md: North-east; south-west; 3.8 km; south-east and north-west.

questions.stem_md:
A student studies the imagined practice sheet, whose scale is 1 cm to 0.5 km. (a) Name the three types of scale and give the form of each for this sheet. [2]

(b) Another sheet has an RF of 1 : 25 000. Write its statement scale. [2]

(c) Using the linear-scale extract, a straight line of 4 blocks of the bar is drawn. State the ground distance and the length in cm on a printed sheet. [3]

(d) Explain which of the two sheets, 1 : 50 000 or 1 : 25 000, shows more detail and give a reason. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Statement scale: 1 cm to 0.5 km. Representative fraction: 1 : 50 000. Linear scale: a bar marked in km.

(b) 25 000 cm = 250 m = 0.25 km, so 1 cm to 0.25 km.

(c) Each block is 1 km, so four blocks are 4 km; on a printed sheet 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 cm.

(d) The 1 : 25 000 sheet is the larger scale: 1 cm stands for a smaller ground distance (0.25 km), so the same area occupies more paper and can show more detail.

questions.solution_md: Three scales; 1 cm to 0.25 km; 4 km and 8 cm; larger scale shows more detail.
